questions.q: Which branch of quantum computing research is most realistically open to a self-taught software engineer without a physics PhD or lab access?
options: Applied/software research — building tooling, running benchmarks, implementing algorithm variants on cloud-accessible hardware
Theoretical research — proving new complexity bounds and designing new error-correcting codes
None of the branches are realistically open without a PhD
Experimental/hardware research — building and characterizing physical qubits in a physics lab
questions.explain: Applied/software research runs on cloud-accessible hardware and simulators and depends on strong software skills rather than lab access or deep theoretical-physics training, making it the realistic entry point for a non-PhD software engineer.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the actual character of most published quantum computing research?
options: Almost entirely theoretical, with no experimental or applied work published
Incremental, bounded improvements and honestly-reported findings, not singular 'breakthroughs'
Dominated by single researchers working completely alone with no team structure
Mostly unpublishable because the field is too new for peer review
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly contrasts popular 'breakthrough' framing with the reality that most published work is incremental -- a specific, bounded claim reported honestly, which is how the field actually advances.

questions.q: In a typical university quantum computing research group, who leads the group and its funding?
options: The most senior PhD student, by seniority
An external industry sponsor who writes the research questions
The principal investigator (PI), usually a professor
A rotating committee of all group members
questions.explain: The lesson describes the PI -- usually a professor -- as the person leading the group, with PhD students, postdocs, and occasionally strong undergraduates or master's students contributing under supervision.

questions.q: What distinguishes experimental/hardware quantum research from the other two branches?
options: It is done entirely on paper with no computers or hardware involved at all
It is the branch most open to non-PhD software engineers
It requires building and characterizing physical qubits, making it the most lab-access- and credential-gated branch
It has no connection to physics or electrical engineering
questions.explain: Experimental/hardware research builds and characterizes physical qubits (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic, neutral-atom) and requires access to a physics lab, which the lesson identifies as the most credential- and access-gated of the three branches.

questions.q: Why does this course's capstone target a 'bounded, honest, incremental contribution' rather than a major breakthrough?
options: Because major breakthroughs are not valuable in quantum computing research
Because the course does not expect students to produce any real results
Because incremental results don't require a hypothesis or experimental design
Because that is how real quantum computing research actually advances, and it matches what a learner can realistically scope and finish
questions.explain: The lesson explains that incremental work is how the field actually progresses, and that framing the capstone this way makes it realistically scopeable and finishable -- a theme the course returns to directly in the capstone-scoping lesson.
